title: Women of Prairie Avenue
premise: Walk south past six houses tied to women who changed Chicago and beyond: nursing, forensic science, a forty-year journal, suffrage, a famous fountain and the street's last great household.

opening.text: WALK: WOMEN OF PRAIRIE AVENUE. Six houses, 1608 to 2115 Prairie, north to south on foot. Each stop names the woman a source ties to the house and why she still matters. Exteriors only; who was home on 1 July 1904 is not claimed.

stops.text: 1608 Prairie, the Frank household in 1904. Henrietta Greenebaum Frank worked for nursing education at the Illinois Training School for Nurses. In 1876 she and her sister Hannah Solomon became the first Jewish members of the Chicago Woman's Club; Hannah went on to found the National Council of Jewish Women.

1700 Prairie, built by the Glessners for their daughter. Frances Glessner Lee later built eighteen tiny crime-scene dioramas, the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, still used to train investigators. She helped found Harvard's Department of Legal Medicine and in 1943 became the first woman police captain in the United States.

1800 Prairie, Glessner House. Frances Macbeth Glessner kept a journal from 1879 for forty years; the house museum writes the family's story from it. In 1904, the year of this scene, she set up a silversmith's workbench in the basement. She also kept bees and ran a Monday Morning Reading Class here from 1893.

1834 Prairie, the Fernando Jones house. Jane Grahame Jones was a longtime and outspoken activist for woman suffrage; her husband's scrapbook keeps clippings on the Illinois Woman Suffrage Association from 1875. In 1913 Illinois became the first state east of the Mississippi to let women vote for president.

2036 Prairie, the Buckingham house, where the 1904 Blue Book lists Clarence Buckingham. In 1927 his sister Kate Sturges Buckingham gave Chicago the Buckingham Fountain in his memory: twice the size of the Versailles fountain it copies, with a centre jet that throws water 150 feet high.

2115 Prairie, the Kelley-Armour house. The 1904 Blue Book lists Mrs. Philip D. Armour here. As the great families died or left for suburbs like Lake Forest she stayed, and the district marker says Armour's widow was among the last residents of the street, dying here in 1927.

endings.text: End of the walk at 2115 Prairie. These are six of the women the sources tie to the avenue; many more lived in its houses unrecorded.

evidence.text: 1700 and 1706 Prairie were twin townhouses John and Frances Glessner built for their two married children; the daughter Frances, married to Blewett Lee in February 1898, moved into 1700 within a few years. George Glessner photographed the pair under construction in 1901.
evidence.locator: The family page's biography of Frances Glessner Lee; the blog's 1901 construction photograph and caption.

evidence.text: Philanthropist and art patron Kate Sturges Buckingham (1858-1937) gave the funds for the fountain, dedicated to her brother, philanthropist and businessman Clarence Buckingham (1854-1913); dedicated 26 August 1927; twice the size of the Latona Basin at Versailles that inspired it; its major display sprays water 150 feet high.
The Clarence Buckingham of the 1904 listing is the Clarence Buckingham (1854-1913) the fountain honours.
evidence.reasoning: The Blue Book lists a Clarence Buckingham in the E. Buckingham household of 2036 Prairie; the fountain honours a Chicago philanthropist and businessman of that name living in 1904 (1854-1913). Same name, same city, same years; no source read here states the identity in words.
